title: The join key
goal: What `+` means, why one key can be both a word and an ending, and where it is used.

blocks.x: Every stroke after the first of a word carries the join key `+` (the `Q` key). A stroke without it always starts a new word. Word boundaries are written explicitly, never inferred.
One key, a word and an ending
The right-hand `D` is both *do* and *-ed*. Only the join key decides which.

head: Strokes
Reads
rows: *end do* (without `+`, the same two keys are two words)

blocks.x: A theory with no join key must give the suffix the bare key (Plover's `-D` is always `{^ed}`), so *do* cannot have it. Here a word and an ending share the key. They do for many:
An ending can be one key, and the commonest words keep the cheapest keys.

items: A continuation stroke (a suffix struck on its own, or the consonants of a syllable that did not fit on the stroke before) is never a word of its own, so it can be as short as one key: [[+-G]] for *-ing*, [[+-D]] for *-ed*. It cannot collide with an unrelated one- or two-key word that has the same letters. See [the suffix table](#/ref/suffixes) and [syllables and folding](#/ref/syllables).
A suffix's own chord reads as its suffix after *any* stroke, dictionary entry or not. See [the solver](#/ref/fallback).
A stem's own outline and a continuation stroke can have the same keys with no clash: only the join key tells them apart.
No vowel has to be dropped to mark a mid-word stroke, so *forget* and *forgot* style pairs never collide because of a boundary.

blocks.x: Keymux learns the join key from the steno layer's config: `extra_keys: ['+']` adds the key and `join_keys: ['+']` marks it as a join key (Keymux 1b9cf76 or later; the key's physical position goes in `layout_overrides`). A stroke with it down is only ever looked up glued onto the strokes before it. When no joined outline matches (`TEST/+-D` does not exist), it falls back to its own entry, and every suffix has one, defined as `{^text}`, so the ending still attaches to the previous word. See [the suffix table](#/ref/suffixes).

Wherever another page says a stroke "joins the one before it", "continues" or is a "continuation stroke", this key is doing it. Every way to build a word with it is on [every way to join a word](#/ref/ways-to-join). Commands, punctuation and fingerspelling are pinned before any word gets an outline: see [reserved strokes](#/ref/reserved-strokes). [Lesson 10](#/lesson/10-endings) teaches endings by hand.
